# Thermodynamically Stable Pair Potentials Beyond the Standard Form

## Overview

In this work, we present examples of thermodynamically stable interaction pair potentials that do not conform to the well-known form consisting of a positive function plus a real continuous function of positive type. These examples are constructed explicitly in dimension one, providing concrete instances that broaden the class of potentials known to satisfy the stability condition.

## Main Results

The central contribution of this text is the demonstration, in dimension one, of pair potentials that are thermodynamically stable yet fall outside the standard characterization mentioned above. This is significant because it shows that the familiar decomposition—a positive function combined with a real continuous function of positive type—is sufficient but not necessary for thermodynamic stability.

Building on the one-dimensional case, we further outline a construction of such a potential in dimension two. This extension confirms that the phenomenon is not restricted to the simplest setting and can be realized in higher dimensions as well.

## Methodological Approach

A notable feature of these constructions is their accessibility. Rather than relying on advanced or sophisticated mathematical machinery, they depend solely on elementary calculations. This makes the results particularly transparent and readily verifiable, allowing the essential ideas to be understood without specialized technical background.

## Theoretical Context

Finally, while the constructions themselves are elementary, the broader mathematical framework that motivates and underlies them deserves separate attention. Accordingly, we address the relevant mathematical background in a distinct discussion, where the deeper structural considerations are explored in greater detail.

# Beyond the Standard Criterion for Thermodynamic Stability of Pair Potentials

## Background and Motivation

In classical statistical mechanics, the concept of *thermodynamic stability* plays a central role in guaranteeing that a system of interacting particles possesses a well-defined thermodynamic limit. A pair potential $\varphi(x)$ is said to be stable if there exists a constant $B \geq 0$ such that, for every finite collection of $N$ particles at positions $x_1, \dots, x_N$, the total interaction energy satisfies

$$
\sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} \varphi(x_i - x_j) \geq -N B.
$$

This inequality prevents the collapse of the system into configurations of arbitrarily negative energy, and it underlies the existence of the pressure, free energy, and other equilibrium quantities in the infinite-volume limit.

A widely used and mathematically convenient sufficient condition for stability is that the potential admit a decomposition of the form

$$
\varphi = \varphi_+ + \psi,
$$

where $\varphi_+$ is a nonnegative function and $\psi$ is a real, continuous function of *positive type*—that is, a function whose Fourier transform is nonnegative, as characterized by Bochner's theorem. This "positive function plus function of positive type" characterization captures a large and important class of stable potentials, and for a long time it has served as the practical benchmark for verifying stability.

## The Problem Addressed

A natural question is whether this standard decomposition exhausts the set of stable potentials, or whether there exist stable interactions that genuinely fall outside this form. If such potentials exist, they would demonstrate that the conventional criterion, while sufficient, is by no means necessary, and that the true space of thermodynamically stable interactions is strictly larger than the class captured by the positive-type decomposition.

The researchers take up precisely this problem. Their goal is to construct explicit, concrete examples of pair potentials that are provably stable yet cannot be represented as the sum of a positive function and a real continuous function of positive type.

## The Constructions

The core contribution consists of building such counterexamples using deliberately elementary and transparent methods. In one spatial dimension, the authors present explicit potentials for which stability can be verified directly, while at the same time showing—through the structure of the potential—that no admissible decomposition into a positive part and a positive-type part can exist. These one-dimensional examples are worked out in full detail, relying only on elementary calculations rather than on heavy functional-analytic machinery.

Building on the one-dimensional case, the authors also outline a construction in two dimensions, indicating how the same essential ideas can be extended to higher-dimensional settings. This demonstrates that the phenomenon is not an artifact peculiar to one dimension but reflects a more general feature of the space of stable potentials.

## Significance

Taken together, these constructions establish that thermodynamic stability can be achieved by potentials that lie strictly beyond the conventional characterization. The existence of such examples clarifies the logical relationship between the standard sufficient condition and the actual property of stability: the positive-type decomposition is only one route to stability among others, and it does not describe the full class of admissible interactions.

The examples presented here are intentionally elementary, chosen so that stability and the failure of the standard decomposition can both be checked by direct computation. The broader mathematical framework that explains *why* such potentials exist—and that situates these examples within a more systematic theory of stability criteria—is developed and discussed separately, leaving the present treatment focused on the explicit, self-contained constructions themselves.

# Thermodynamic Principles in Modern Construction

The field of construction has evolved dramatically over the past several decades, incorporating scientific principles that were once confined to laboratories and academic institutions. Among the most influential of these principles is **thermodynamic** theory, which governs how heat and energy move through building materials and spaces.

## Understanding Thermodynamic Applications

Thermodynamic laws describe the transfer, transformation, and conservation of energy. In the context of building design, these laws help engineers predict how structures will respond to temperature changes, humidity, and energy demands. By applying thermodynamic principles, architects and builders can create environments that remain comfortable while minimizing energy consumption.

For example, the way heat flows from warmer areas to cooler ones directly influences decisions about insulation, ventilation, and window placement. Understanding these dynamics allows for smarter, more efficient design choices.

## Thermodynamic Considerations in Construction

The **construction** industry has embraced thermodynamic concepts to improve sustainability and reduce operating costs. Modern buildings are designed with careful attention to:

- **Insulation systems** that limit unwanted heat transfer
- **Thermal mass** materials that store and release energy gradually
- **Passive solar design** that harnesses natural energy sources
- **Efficient HVAC systems** that manage indoor climates responsibly

Each of these elements reflects a deeper understanding of how energy behaves within a physical structure. Construction professionals now collaborate closely with engineers to ensure that thermodynamic efficiency is built into projects from the earliest planning stages.

## Why These Principles Matter

**These** advancements are not merely technical curiosities—they carry significant real-world consequences. Buildings account for a substantial portion of global energy consumption, and improving their thermal performance can dramatically reduce environmental impact. These improvements also translate into lower utility bills, greater occupant comfort, and longer-lasting structures.

As climate concerns intensify and energy costs rise, these thermodynamic-informed approaches will become increasingly essential. The integration of scientific rigor into construction practices represents a promising path toward a more sustainable and efficient built environment.

## Conclusion

The marriage of thermodynamic science and construction expertise has transformed how we design and build. By respecting these fundamental principles of energy and heat, the industry continues to create structures that serve both people and the planet more effectively than ever before.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a mathematical physics paper about constructing thermodynamically stable pair potentials that are not of the form "positive function plus function of positive type."
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

A pair potential $\varphi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$ is called *stable* if there is a constant $B\ge 0$ such that
$$
\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}\varphi(x_i-x_j)\ \ge\ -BN
$$
for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and every configuration $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb{R}^d$. Stability is the basic hypothesis guaranteeing a well-defined thermodynamic limit in classical statistical mechanics. The most widely used sufficient condition, due in essence to Fisher and Ruelle, asserts stability whenever $\varphi$ admits a decomposition $\varphi=\varphi_+ + \psi$, where $\varphi_+\ge 0$ and $\psi$ is a function of positive type (equivalently, $\widehat\psi\ge 0$). It has long been recognized that this decomposition is sufficient but not necessary, yet explicit stable potentials provably lying outside this class have been scarce.

In this paper we construct explicit families of stable pair potentials that do *not* admit any decomposition of the form "positive function plus function of positive type." Our examples are continuous, of compact support, and can be taken smooth; they are stable for reasons that cannot be captured by the positive-type mechanism. The obstruction is made quantitative through a duality argument: we show that membership in the Fisher–Ruelle class is equivalent to a separation property in a suitable cone of measures, and we produce potentials whose associated energy functionals are bounded below while violating this separation. The construction combines a spectral analysis of the Fourier transform on a lattice of scales with a perturbation scheme that preserves lower energy bounds while destroying positive-definiteness of every admissible "positive-type part."

As a consequence, the class of Fisher–Ruelle potentials is strictly smaller than the class of stable potentials, and we quantify the gap by estimating how far our examples lie from the Fisher–Ruelle cone in natural norms. We discuss implications for stability criteria based on Fourier positivity, for the analysis of soft-core and oscillatory interactions, and for the general problem of characterizing stability intrinsically. Several open questions concerning the closure and convexity properties of the set of stable potentials are formulated in light of these examples.

# Abstract

We present elementary constructions of stable pair potentials in dimensions one and two. A pair potential is called stable if the total interaction energy of any finite configuration of particles is bounded below by a linear function of the number of particles—a condition of fundamental importance in classical statistical mechanics, where it guarantees the existence of the thermodynamic limit. While stability is often verified through sufficient conditions such as positive-definiteness or the presence of a hard core, we focus instead on producing explicit, transparent examples that can be analyzed directly. Using only elementary techniques, we exhibit families of continuous pair potentials on the line and in the plane whose stability follows from straightforward estimates, avoiding appeals to Fourier analysis or more advanced machinery. Our examples illustrate the interplay between the geometry of low-dimensional configurations and the algebraic structure of the potential, and clarify the boundary between stable and non-stable interactions. These constructions are intended to be accessible and to serve as instructive models for further study.

# Abstract

Thermodynamic stability of pairwise interaction potentials is a foundational requirement for the existence of a well-defined thermodynamic limit, and a widely cited sufficient condition asserts that stability follows whenever the potential possesses a nonnegative Fourier transform combined with a suitably repulsive short-range core. In this work, we construct explicit counterexamples demonstrating that this condition, as commonly stated in the literature, fails to guarantee stability when the regularity assumptions on the potential are relaxed. Specifically, we exhibit a family of continuous, integrable potentials satisfying the nominal spectral positivity criterion for which the N-body energy is not bounded below by a linear function of the particle number, thereby violating the Ruelle stability bound. Our results clarify the precise hypotheses under which the sufficient condition remains valid and caution against its uncritical application in models arising in soft-matter physics and statistical mechanics.
